title: Error Enhancement in Physical Rehabilitation: From Motor Learning Theory to Robotic Neurorehabilitation– A Comprehensive Review
content: Error enhancement (EE), also referred to as error augmentation (EA), represents a distinctive ap-proach to motor rehabilitation in which errors are not minimized but deliberately magnified in a controlled manner. The underlying premise is derived from contemporary theories of motor learning and sensorimotor adaptation: when the nervous system detects a discrepancy between the intended and actual consequences of a movement, this error provides a powerful teaching signal that can modify subsequent motor commands. Robotic systems make it possible to manipulate this error precisely by applying externally generated forces that deviate the limb from its intended trajectory. This review examines the theoretical basis of error enhancement, its development as a rehabilitation strategy in particular attention is given to studies conducted in healthy individuals and stroke survivors. The available evidence is then considered in relation to sensorimotor inte-gration, virtual reality, constraint-induced movement therapy, and the Bobath concept. Finally, the emergence of the BioXtreme/deXtreme robotic platform is discussed as a translational development that combines robotic force-field manipulation, three-dimensional movement, virtual reality and adaptive error enhancement. Although the evidence remains preliminary and larger controlled trials are required, error enhancement provides a compelling framework for converting movement error from a problem to be suppressed into a signal that can actively drive motor adaptation and rehabilitation.
